lead: Machine parts fail in different ways depending on whether the material is ductile or brittle, and on whether the load is steady, repeated or sudden. This unit turns a complicated three-dimensional stress state into one number that can be compared with a material strength, adds the effect of notches, and builds the fatigue criteria used to size shafts, springs and gears.
about: This unit answers one question: given a part and its loads, will it survive? The chapter on theories of failure reduces a combined stress state to one equivalent stress and compares it with the material's strength, separately for ductile and brittle materials. Stress concentration adds the local rise at holes, grooves and fillets. The fatigue chapter explains how repeated stress breaks a part below yield and gives the S–N curve, the endurance limit and finite-life design. Fluctuating stresses puts mean and alternating stress on one diagram with the Soderberg, Goodman and Gerber lines. The last chapter, taught in only a few universities, covers loads applied suddenly or dropped from a height.

chapters.idea: A complicated combined stress state can be replaced by one equivalent stress that is compared with the yield strength (ductile) or the ultimate strength (brittle).
chapters.depth: Define the three principal stresses with σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ σ3. Give five theories, each with its equivalent stress: Rankine or maximum principal stress, σeq = σ1; St Venant or maximum principal strain; Tresca, Coulomb or maximum shear stress, σeq = σ1 − σ3; von Mises or maximum distortion energy, σeq = √(σ1² − σ1σ2 + σ2²) for plane stress; Coulomb–Mohr for brittle materials with different strengths in tension and compression. Factor of safety n = Syt/σeq for ductile, Sut/σeq for brittle. Show the biaxial picture: the Tresca hexagon sits inside the von Mises ellipse, so Tresca is conservative. State the choice rule and note that design codes prefer von Mises. Derive the von Mises form in terms of σx, σy, τxy: σeq = √(σx² − σxσy + σy² + 3τxy²).

figure.title: Choosing a failure theory
figure.aria: A flow chart from the three principal stresses through a material-type decision into the brittle or ductile theory, ending in one equivalent stress checked against the allowable strength.

chapters.example: A steel shaft with yield strength Syt = 400 MPa carries a combined load that gives σx = 100 MPa, σy = 40 MPa and τxy = 60 MPa; the third principal stress is zero. Find σ1 and σ3, then the factor of safety by Tresca and by von Mises. Answer: mean stress 70 MPa, radius of Mohr's circle √(30² + 60²) = 67.1 MPa, so σ1 = 137.1 MPa, σ2 = 2.9 MPa, σ3 = 0. Tresca: n = 400/137.1 = 2.92. Von Mises: σeq = √(137.1² − 137.1×2.9 + 2.9²) = 135.6 MPa, n = 400/135.6 = 2.95.
chapters.trap: Keeping σ3 = 0 when the third principal stress is actually compressive, and comparing a ductile material with Sut instead of Syt. Ductile materials are checked against yield strength, brittle materials against ultimate strength.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: principal stresses from combined and eccentric loading, and the factor of safety.
chapters.leave: Fracture mechanics and the full Coulomb–Mohr envelope with compressive strength. Shaft sizing with these theories is Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A hole, groove or fillet raises the local stress by a factor Kt, and notch sensitivity q tells you how much of that rise the material actually feels.
chapters.depth: Define Kt = σmax/σnom and insist that σnom is taken on the net section, separately for axial, bending and torsion. Standard values to know: Kt = 3 for a small circular hole in a wide plate in tension; values for a shoulder fillet rise as r/d falls; a keyway or a sharp thread root is severe. Explain why charts exist and how to read them, not memorize them. Notch sensitivity q between 0 and 1, with Kf = 1 + q(Kt − 1) as the fatigue notch factor; give q = 1/(1 + √a/√r), where √a is the Neuber constant in √mm and r is the notch radius in mm. Under static load a ductile material yields locally and Kt may be ignored; a brittle material and every fatigue case use Kf. List the fixes: larger fillet radius, gradual section change, relief groove, avoiding sharp keyway corners.

figure.aria: Three straight lines of fatigue notch factor against theoretical stress concentration factor for notch sensitivity zero, one half and one; the q = 1 line is the full diagonal.

chapters.example: A stepped shaft has d = 40 mm, D = 50 mm and fillet radius r = 4 mm, and carries a steady bending moment M = 300 N·m. The chart gives Kt = 1.8 and the notch sensitivity at this radius is q = 0.85. Find the nominal stress, the peak stress and the fatigue notch factor. Answer: σnom = 32M/(πd³) = 32 × 300 000/(π × 40³) = 47.8 MPa. Peak stress = Kt σnom = 85.9 MPa. Kf = 1 + 0.85(1.8 − 1) = 1.68, so the stress that matters in fatigue is 1.68 × 47.8 = 80.2 MPa.
chapters.trap: Using Kt in a fatigue calculation instead of Kf, and taking the nominal stress on the gross area when the chart was drawn for the net area.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 bending and torsional stress formulas; Chapter 2.1 for how a local stress is finally compared with strength.
chapters.leave: Contact stress concentration between rollers and races, which belongs to Unit 5. Detailed chart families are looked up, not derived.

chapters.idea: A stress repeated many times cracks the part even though it is below yield, and the S–N curve gives the stress amplitude that survives a stated number of cycles.
chapters.depth: Mechanism in three stages: slip bands and crack initiation at a stress raiser, slow crack growth across the section, then fast final fracture. Beach marks on the fracture face, striations under the microscope. The rotating bending test (R. R. Moore) gives a fully reversed constant amplitude; plot S against N on log–log axes: S = A N^b, through 0.9Sut at 10³ cycles and Se at 10⁶ cycles. Ferrous metals show a knee and a true endurance limit; aluminium and most non-ferrous metals do not. Se' = 0.5Sut for steels up to about Sut = 1400 MPa. Marin factors: ka surface finish, kb size, kc load type, kd temperature, ke reliability, so Se = ka kb kc kd ke Se'. Finite life from the same straight line. Surface treatment, polishing and shot peening raise fatigue strength; corrosion and sharp notches lower it.

figure.aria: An S–N line falling from 540 MPa at a thousand cycles to 230 MPa at a million cycles and then staying flat as the endurance limit.

chapters.example: A machined steel shaft has Sut = 600 MPa, surface factor ka = 0.85, size factor kb = 0.90, and load, temperature and reliability factors of 1. Find the endurance limit, then the life at a fully reversed stress amplitude of 300 MPa. Answer: Se' = 0.5 × 600 = 300 MPa; Se = 0.85 × 0.90 × 300 = 230 MPa. The line runs from (10³, 540 MPa) to (10⁶, 230 MPa), giving slope b = −0.1236 per decade. At 300 MPa, log N = 5.07, so N ≈ 1.16 × 10⁵ cycles.
chapters.trap: Quoting Se' = 0.5Sut as the design endurance limit and forgetting the Marin factors, and applying an endurance limit to a part made of aluminium, which has none.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 for Kf; Unit 1 for the fully reversed bending stress in the test specimen.
chapters.leave: Cumulative damage with Miner's rule and variable amplitude load spectra. Bearing life in Unit 5 and gear life in Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Put mean stress on one axis and alternating stress on the other, draw a failure line between the endurance limit and the static strength, and keep the working point below it.
chapters.depth: σmax, σmin, σm = (σmax + σmin)/2, σa = (σmax − σmin)/2, and R = σmin/σmax. Four lines on the σa–σm diagram: modified Goodman or Haigh, σa/Se + σm/Sut = 1; Soderberg, σa/Se + σm/Syt = 1; Gerber parabola, σa/Se + (σm/Sut)² = 1; Langer yield line, σa + σm = Syt. Factor of safety: Goodman and Soderberg give 1/n = σa/Se + σm/Sut (or Syt) with σa and σm both multiplied by n; Gerber needs a quadratic in n. Order of conservatism: Soderberg safest, Goodman next, Gerber closest to test data for ductile steels. Apply Kf to σa, and follow your textbook on whether it also multiplies σm. For combined bending and torsion, build an equivalent σa and τa first. Mention the ASME elliptic line as a code version.

figure.aria: Three failure lines starting at an alternating stress of 230 MPa; the Soderberg line falls fastest to 400 MPa mean stress, the Goodman line reaches 600 MPa, and the Gerber parabola bows outward between them.

chapters.example: A shaft section sees σmax = 120 MPa and σmin = 40 MPa. The material has Sut = 600 MPa, Syt = 400 MPa and Se = 230 MPa. Find the factor of safety by Goodman, Soderberg and Gerber. Answer: σm = 80 MPa, σa = 40 MPa. Goodman: 1/n = 40/230 + 80/600 = 0.1739 + 0.1333, n = 3.25. Soderberg: 1/n = 0.1739 + 80/400 = 0.3739, n = 2.67. Gerber: 0.01777n² + 0.1739n − 1 = 0 gives n = 4.06.
chapters.trap: Swapping the axes — σa is vertical and σm is horizontal — and pairing the wrong strength with the wrong line: Goodman uses Sut, Soderberg uses Syt.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3 for Se and the S–N curve; Chapter 2.1 for combining bending and torsion into equivalent stresses.
chapters.leave: Cumulative damage and multiaxial fatigue criteria. Shaft design under combined bending and torsion is Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A load applied suddenly or dropped from a height stretches the part further than the same load applied slowly, and the dynamic factor follows from the energy it must absorb.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Compare three cases for an axial member: slowly applied load, suddenly applied load (dynamic factor 2), and a weight falling through height h, where δ = δst(1 + √(1 + 2h/δst)) and the stress follows the same factor. Show the energy basis, U = ½Pδ = σ²V/(2E), and the equivalence of the two views: work done by the falling weight equals strain energy stored. Give δst = WL/(AE) for a rod and the bending equivalent from Unit 1. Define modulus of resilience as the strain energy at yield and modulus of toughness as the energy to fracture. Mention shock loading as a repeated sudden load, handled with a service factor over the static design, and why a spring or a rubber pad is used to soften impact.

figure.aria: A rising curve of dynamic factor against the drop height divided by the static extension; it starts at 2 for a suddenly applied load and grows with the square root of the height ratio.

chapters.example: A 500 N weight falls 50 mm onto a collar at the lower end of a vertical steel rod of diameter 20 mm and length 1 m, with E = 200 GPa. Find the maximum extension and the maximum stress. Answer: A = 314.2 mm², δst = WL/(AE) = 500 × 1000/(314.2 × 200 000) = 0.00796 mm. Then √(1 + 2 × 50/0.00796) = 112.1, so δ = 0.00796 × 113.1 = 0.90 mm and σ = Eδ/L = 200 000 × 0.90/1000 = 180 MPa. The static stress was only 1.59 MPa.
chapters.trap: Treating a suddenly applied load as static — the factor is 2, not 1 — and mixing millimetres with metres inside δst, which throws the square-root term far off.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for axial and bending deflection and strain energy; Chapter 2.1 for comparing the resulting stress with the material strength.
chapters.leave: Vibration, resonance and the critical speed of shafts after impact, which belong to Unit 3.
